subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Concurrency for Acme — Next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
To: Raj Patel <raj.patel@acme.com>
Cc: David Kim <david_kim@redwood.com>, Ethan Park <ethan_park@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-03-02T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Concurrency for Acme — Next steps

Thanks again for the time today, Raj — good call. Quick recap and proposed next steps from our performance/SLO discussion: 

Summary of what we heard from Acme: 
- Latency targets: 95th percentile <= 200ms for typical short completions (<=512 tokens); streaming required for long-form generation and real-time updates.
- Sustained throughput: ~200 requests/sec across the fleet during normal business hours.
- Peak bursts: spikes up to ~500 rps for ~30-60s during batch jobs/cron-driven runs.
- Concurrency: concurrent in-flight requests expected between 800-1,000 during peaks (this is across all app instances).
- Connection pattern: client-side connection pooling with ~150 concurrent connections per app cluster node; multi-region failover is planned but initial traffic is US-only.

Redwood's immediate asks / what we need from you: 
1) Confirm the 95p/99p latency targets you care about and give us examples of payload sizes (avg tokens in / out).
2) Share a simple traffic matrix (typical rps per endpoint + expected burst characteristics).
3) If you plan to use streaming (SSE/WebSocket), tell us whether you'll use chunked responses or keep an open websocket per user session.

What we can offer / proposed short-term plan: 
- Sandbox quota bump: we can temporarily increase concurrency quota to 1,200 concurrent requests and allow bursts to 600 rps for load testing.
- Engineering sync: loop in our infra/serving team (David and Ethan) to validate connection counts and recommend client-side pooling settings.
- Long-term: recommend Dedicated (reserved capacity) if you need predictable 99.9% latency SLOs at sustained 200+ rps — we'll move to a capacity quote and procurement path.

Attachments: Acme-SLOs-draft.pdf (draft SLO sheet), concurrency-calculator.xlsx (simple calculator).

Proposed next steps: 
- Can you confirm the traffic matrix by EOD Wed?
- Would Thu/ Fri next week at 10am PT work for a technical sync with your platform/infra team + our serving engineers?

Thanks — I'll follow up with a proposed calendar invite once I hear back.

—Marissa

Thanks Marissa — that all looks right. A few clarifications / asks from our side: 
- Tokens: avg request ~120 input tokens, avg response ~180 tokens. For some long-form customer messages we'll hit ~1,200 output tokens and will rely on streaming.
- Traffic matrix (quick): baseline 150 rps, typical spikes 450 rps (few minutes), scheduled batch windows up to 700 rps for ~10 minutes.
- Concurrency: we estimate ~6 app servers in the first phase, each holding up to ~160 concurrent outbound requests in the pool => ~960 concurrent in-flight requests.
- Connection pooling: we plan to reuse HTTP/1.1 keep-alive connections, with ~40 connections per server to the Redwood endpoint. We prefer not to open a websocket per user — we'll use chunked HTTP streaming.

Ask: can Redwood support a sustained concurrency quota of 1,000 and let us burst to 700 rps during scheduled jobs? We'd prefer to avoid Dedicated if the quota can be raised with predictable pricing.

Also, can you provide a sample load-test endpoint + short instructions so our infra team can run a dry run?

—Raj

Subject: Re: Post-call: Performance SLOs & Concurrency for Acme — Next steps

Looping in a few quick engineering notes before our sync — high-level recommendations based on the traffic you described: 
- Use HTTP/1.1 keep-alive with connection pooling; TCP/TLS handshake costs are non-trivial at scale.
- Aim for ~30-50 connections per app server to the Redwood endpoint if you have efficient multiplexing in your client. With 6 servers, 50x6 = 300 physical connections which is fine.
- Concurrency per connection: we recommend limiting concurrent requests per connection to 2-4 depending on your client library and whether you're streaming. Streaming is best with 1 request per connection to avoid head-of-line blocking.
- For chunked streaming, set a read buffer flush interval (~50-100ms) so partial tokens are delivered promptly without excessive network churn.
- Backoff: implement jittered exponential backoff and 429 handling; Redwood will return a structured quota error when the temporary limit is hit.

I'll bring detailed load-test guidance and a simple curl/vegeta example to the call.

—David
Senior Software Engineer, Serving Runtime | Redwood Inference
